newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexicans jubilant as PRI suffers nationwide blow.
newsitem.headline: Mexicans jubilant as PRI suffers nationwide blow.

text.p: Jubilant Mexicans took to the streets early on Monday to celebrate an unprecedented election upset that saw Mexico's ruling party lose control of the capital city and the lower house of Congress.

Preliminary results showed that the Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) was trounced by a left-wing opponent in Mexico City and had lost its majority in the Chamber of Deputies for the first time in its 68-year history.
But President Ernesto Zedillo took the bad news in his stride, focusing instead on what most Mexicans celebrated -- the taking hold of democracy in a country long dominated by a one-party system.

Zedillo held out a friendly hand to Cuauhtemoc Cardenas, the PRI's arch-enemy who was elected mayor of Mexico City after two unsuccessful presidential bids that made him a symbol of the fight to pry open the PRI's monopoly on power.
"Mexico has made an irreversible, definitive, historic step toward becoming a normal democracy," a smiling Zedillo said on national television.
"I want to congratulate Mr. Cuauhtemoc Cardenas very sincerely...I wish him the best success in his delicate task."

Residents of the huge metropolis broke out into wild celebrations, and the majestic main square -- second in size only to Moscow's Red Square -- became a sea of yellow flags, beaming faces and V-for-victory signs.
"Cuauhtemoc, Cuauhtemoc," yelled thousands of supporters of Cardenas's Party of the Democratic Revolution (PRD). Many faces were painted with yellow Aztec suns, the party emblem.
"There's no doubt about it. The PRD has won the city, everything points to it. Let's now get ready to win in 2000," Cardenas told the crowd, pointing to a third bid for the presidency in that year.

Voter anger at a deep economic crisis and a string of high-profile corruption scandals fuelled the suprise swing to the left and the recovery of Cardenas' party from the brink of collapse a few years ago.
The PRI lost its grip on the lower house of Congress that it had held since its founding in 1929, preliminary results showed.

That threatened to make life more difficult for Zedillo to hammer through ambitious economic reforms, and economists admitted Wall Street -- which has billions of dollars staked on stability in Mexico's financial markets -- may have underestimated the impact of such a huge Cardenas victory.

With 70 percent of the votes counted, the PRI had 37.31 percent, well short of the 42 percent needed to keep the majority that for decades has made the Mexican Congress little more than a rubber stamp for presidential rule.

It was also headed for defeat in the race for governor of Mexico's richest industrial state of Nuevo Leon, and one of its prize political fighters, ex-party president Fernando Ortiz Arana, was unexpectedly beaten in the central state of Queretaro, results showed.
Both those races were won by the conservative National Action Party (PAN), but this party's position as Mexico's second strongest party was hotly challenged by the PRD.
In the national race for the chamber of deputies, the PAN had 27.66 percent and the PRD 26.23 percent.
The PAN's candidate in Mexico City, Carlos Castillo Peraza, polled just 16.20 percent of the vote, compared to the PRI's 25.30 percent, and Cardenas' whopping 47.70 percent.
Most of the 52 million registered voters cast their ballots in peace, though some irregularities were reported at some of the 104,700 polling stations.

The worst problems came in the southern state of Chiapas, where mobs of angry Indians -- some wearing the trademabrk facemasks of the Zapatista rebel army -- burned or destroyed scores of polling booths and blocked roads.

Independent watchdog group Alianza Civica said 610 polling stations of 3,520 scheduled to take votes failed to open because of the attacks, and the Federal Electoral Institute said results in one electoral district near the Zapatista zone of control may be annuled because of the troubles.
Zapatista chief Subcommander Marcos called on the Indians last week to boycott the elections to protest against what he termed the "militarization" of the region by the government.
The Zapatistas led an armed uprising in Chiapas three years ago and peace talks have not settled the dispute.
